title: Gridded ion thruster
description: No combustion at all. Electricity strips electrons from xenon atoms, and an electric field between two grids fires the ions out at about 40 km/s. The thrust is tiny, about the weight of a few sheets of paper, but it uses propellant ten times more sparingly than any chemical engine and can run for years.

reference.engine: NASA NEXT-C (flown on the DART spacecraft)

derived.note: overall size and internal layout are representative

reference.note: The 0.36 m beam diameter matches the published figure. The overall size and internal layout are representative, the grid holes are drawn far larger and fewer than the real ones, and the tank and power unit are schematic.

flow_model.caption: Xenon gas drifts slowly into the chamber, is ionised there, and is flung out through the grids at about 40 km/s, more than ten times faster than any chemical exhaust. Streak speeds are on a compressed scale.
flow_model.note: Xenon and electron speeds are nominal. Ion speed follows from the published specific impulse.

parts.title: Xenon tank
parts.description: Stores the propellant, the inert gas xenon, at high pressure. An ion thruster uses so little of it that a small tank lasts for years. Shown schematically, not to scale.

parts.title: Flow controller
parts.description: Meters a trickle of xenon into the thruster: a few milligrams per second.

parts.title: Power processing unit
parts.description: Converts the spacecraft's solar power into the voltages the thruster needs, up to 1,800 V across the grids. Shown schematically, not to scale.

parts.title: Power harness
parts.description: Cables from the power unit to the thruster and its neutralizer.

parts.title: Mount
parts.description: Fixes the thruster to the spacecraft, usually on a gimbal so the thrust can be aimed.

parts.title: Plasma screen
parts.description: Grounded outer shell. It keeps the high-voltage parts inside from attracting stray electrons from space.

parts.title: Propellant manifold
parts.description: Ring that releases the xenon gas evenly into the back of the chamber.

parts.title: Discharge cathode
parts.description: Emits electrons into the chamber. They collide with xenon atoms and knock an electron off each, turning the gas into positively charged ions.

parts.title: Magnet rings
parts.description: Permanent magnets around the chamber. Their field makes the electrons spiral instead of flying straight to the wall, so each one ionises more xenon.

parts.title: Discharge chamber
parts.description: Where the xenon is ionised. The wall is the anode that collects the electrons.

parts.title: Grid mount
parts.description: Holds the two grids a fraction of a millimetre apart on ceramic insulators.

parts.title: Screen grid
parts.description: First of two perforated grids. Ions drift into its thousands of holes from the chamber side.

parts.title: Accelerator grid
parts.description: Held at a strongly negative voltage. The electric field between the two grids accelerates each ion to about 40 km/s. This is the thruster's nozzle.

parts.title: Front mask
parts.description: Closes the gap between the grids and the plasma screen.

parts.title: Neutralizer
parts.description: A second cathode beside the beam. It adds electrons to the departing ions, so the spacecraft does not build up a charge that would pull the ions back.
